title: AI-assisted literature screening: A hybrid approach using large language models and retrieval-augmented generation.
design: AI-assisted literature screening: A hybrid approach using large language models and retrieval-augmented generation.
data: A corpus of 6331 biomedical articles, focusing on identifying literature discussing the applications of LLMs in patient care using Electronic Health Record (EHR) data.
method: A hybrid approach combining rule-based preprocessing with DeepSeek R1 using RAG prompting (rule + DeepSeek-reasoner@Prompt II), and exploring ensemble strategies.
comparator: Traditional manual screening of articles retrieved through keyword search.
results: Recall (sensitivity)=0.77; Accuracy=0.88; Time efficiency=LLMs offer the potential to automate the screening process, which is time-consuming and difficult to scale with traditional methods.
main_finding: The hybrid approach combining rule-based preprocessing with DeepSeek R1 using RAG prompting (rule + DeepSeek-reasoner@Prompt II) achieved the best overall performance among individual models, with a precision of 0.34, recall of 0.77, NPV of 1.00, and g-mean of 0.87. Ensemble methods outperformed this approach greatly in precision, achieving a perfect score of 1.00 in the main use case, but showed comparable performance across other metrics, with the exception of F1. In generalizability tests, DeepSeek-R1 achieved the highest F1-score (0.93) and accuracy (0.88) across additional topics, whereas ensemble methods did not show substantial improvement.

title: Evaluation of a Prompt-Standardized LLM Pipeline for Title–Abstract Screening: Cross-Domain Performance and Error Taxonomy
design: Evaluation of a Prompt-Standardized LLM Pipeline for Title–Abstract Screening: Cross-Domain Performance and Error Taxonomy. Purpose. This project evaluates whether a large language model (LLM) can safely assist the title–abstract screening stage of systematic reviews using a sensitivity-first, negative-triage policy. We focus on prompt design and reproducible governance rather than model retraining, asking: (i) how well a governed LLM generalizes across very different review types, and (ii) whether a single, pre-specified prompt refinement can predictably shift recall/specificity.
data: We performed a retrospective replay of Gemini 2.5 Pro against adjudicated abstract-stage labels from four completed reviews selected a priori to maximize heterogeneity: (R1) artificial sweeteners (clinical nutrition), (R2) mesenchymal stem cells + scaffold in burn models (preclinical), (R3) dengue diagnostics (clinical accuracy), and (R4) vitamin C randomized trials in arthroplasty (rare-positive). No fine-tuning or retrieval was used.
method: For each corpus we computed confusion matrices and standard metrics (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, accuracy), and conducted a cross-domain error taxonomy of false positives/negatives. Based on pre-specified rules, we ran one prompt optimization introducing early “hard gates” (publication type/setting), minimal sufficient PICO checks, and an explicit tie-break favoring inclusion under ambiguity, then re-evaluated.
results: Baseline performance varied by domain (high recall in broad clinical/diagnostic tasks; poor recall in a tightly scoped preclinical task; moderate under extreme class imbalance). title: Accuracy of Large Language Models for Literature Screening in Thoracic Surgery: Diagnostic Study.
design: Diagnostic study comparing the accuracy of LLM-assisted screening versus manual literature screening across 6 thoracic surgery meta-analyses.
method: LLM-assisted screening using ChatGPT-4o (OpenAI), Claude-3.5 (Anthropic) sonnet, and Gemini-1.5 pro (Google) for resolving discrepancies
results: pooled sensitivity=0.73 (95% CI 0.57-0.85); pooled specificity=0.99 (95% CI 0.97-0.99); area under the curve (AUC)=0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.99)
main_finding: LLMs outperformed traditional machine learning-based tools (ASReview and Abstrackr) in both sensitivity and AUC values, suggesting that LLMs offer a more accurate and efficient approach to literature screening.

title: Evaluating Prompting Strategies and Large Language Models in Systematic Literature Review Screening: Relevance and Task-Stage Classification
design: The study evaluates prompting strategies and large language models (LLMs) in systematic literature review (SLR) screening, focusing on relevance and task-stage classification. The methodology includes dataset construction, prompting strategy design, model selection, and evaluation metrics. The dataset was curated from academic publications on SLR automation, with 1,376 unique studies manually screened for eligibility.
data: The dataset includes 1,376 unique studies manually screened for eligibility, which addressed automation of any SLR stage (searching, screening, retrieval, synthesis, report writing).
method: The study evaluates six state-of-the-art LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-Mini, DeepSeek-Chat-V3, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-3.5-Haiku, and Llama-4-Maverick) under four prompting strategies (zero-shot, few-shot, CoT, and CoT-few-shot).
comparator: The study compares LLMs with human reviewers, as the dataset was annotated by two researchers with LLM and systematic-review experience, resolving disagreements by consensus.
results: Recall=Recall is defined as the proportion of true positives among all actual positives (model sensitivity).; Precision=Precision is defined as the proportion of true positives among all predicted positives (model specificity).; Accuracy=Accuracy is reported for relevance classification, with GPT-4o and DeepSeek delivering more stable results, ranking highest in accuracy, precision, and F1 while maintaining strong recall (>0.925).; Time efficiency=The study highlights the operational constraints of screening, noting that screening typically spans tens of thousands of abstracts, and token-expanding prompts materially increase spend and latency.
main_finding: The study finds that CoT-few-shot prompting yields the most reliable precision–recall balance, zero-shot maximizes recall for high-sensitivity passes, and self-reflection underperforms due to over-inclusivity and instability across models. GPT-4o and DeepSeek provide robust overall performance, while GPT-4o-mini performs competitively at a substantially lower dollar cost.
limitations: The study acknowledges that self-reflection prompting underperforms due to over-inclusivity and instability across models. Additionally, the study notes that model choice can vary costs by several orders of magnitude, and token-expanding prompts materially increase spend and latency.
